title: Trauma to the Brain and Spinal Cord
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains what mechanical force does to the brain and spinal cord and how each injury produces its signs. It moves from functional injury (concussion) to structural injury (contusion and diffuse axonal injury), then to the expanding hematoma that kills through rising intracranial pressure and herniation, and finally to spinal cord transection and compression. Board questions give a mechanism of injury, a time course, or a pattern of signs and ask you to name the lesion, its level, or what happens next. Reasoning from the vessel torn, the tissue sheared, and the structure compressed answers most of them.
prerequisites: Meninges, dural partitions, and the potential epidural and subdural spaces (NE-4)
Course of the oculomotor nerve and the corticospinal tract through the midbrain (NE-7, NE-8)
Cerebral blood flow, autoregulation, and cerebral perfusion pressure (NE-10)
Spinal cord segments, the reflex arc, and upper versus lower motor neuron signs (NE-3, NE-5)
Sympathetic outflow from T1 to L2 and sacral parasympathetic outflow from S2 to S4 (NE-9)

connections.how: The anatomy of epidural and subdural hematomas is taught there; this chapter follows what happens once either becomes a mass.
Traumatic hematomas and contusions raise intracranial pressure by the same pressure-volume rules and herniate through the same dural openings.
Chronic traumatic encephalopathy is a tauopathy whose distribution of tau separates it from Alzheimer disease.
Vertebral metastases and spinal epidural abscess are the main nontraumatic causes of cord and cauda equina compression.
Loss of descending control of sympathetic and sacral parasympathetic neurons explains neurogenic shock, bladder failure, and autonomic dysreflexia.

terms.def: A traumatic, rapidly resolving disturbance of brain function with no lesion on standard CT or MRI.
A bruise of the brain: hemorrhage and necrosis in cortex, centered on the crests of gyri, where the brain struck the skull.
Contusion beneath the point of impact (coup) and on the opposite side of the brain (contrecoup).
Widespread axonal damage caused by rotational shear, producing coma without a mass lesion.
A bulbous swelling where transported material accumulates at a point of axonal damage; also called a retraction ball.
Because the skull is rigid, any increase in one intracranial volume (brain, blood, or CSF) must be offset by a decrease in another or pressure rises.
The pressure driving blood through the brain, equal to mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
Displacement of the medial temporal lobe through the tentorial notch, compressing the oculomotor nerve and midbrain.
Hemorrhage in the midline midbrain and pons from tearing of paramedian basilar branches as the brainstem is pushed downward.
The temporary loss of all reflex activity, tone, and autonomic function below an acute cord lesion.
The dermatome below which sensation is lost on the trunk or limbs, marking a lesion of the spinal cord.
The bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots within the thecal sac below the end of the spinal cord.

sections.title: Concussion, postconcussion syndrome, and chronic traumatic encephalopathy

blocks.text: Concussion is a traumatic brain injury in which force transmitted to the head causes a rapid-onset, short-lived disturbance of neurologic function that resolves on its own. Typical features are confusion, amnesia for the event, headache, dizziness, nausea, and slowed thinking. Loss of consciousness, when it happens, is brief and is not required. Standard CT and MRI are normal, and that is the defining point: concussion is a disorder of function, not a visible lesion. A focal deficit or an abnormal scan means contusion, hemorrhage, or axonal injury instead.

The disturbance is metabolic. Sudden acceleration stretches neuronal membranes and axons, mechanically opened channels let K+ leave and Na+ and Ca2+ enter, and depolarized neurons release a surge of glutamate that spreads the depolarization. Restoring ion gradients drives the Na+/K+ ATPase hard and sharply increases glucose use, at the same time that cerebral blood flow falls. Ca2+ taken up by mitochondria further limits ATP production. This supply and demand mismatch explains symptoms in a structurally intact brain, and it is why a second blow before recovery is complete can cause disproportionate injury. Most people recover within days to a few weeks.

blocks.title: Neurometabolic cascade of concussion
steps: Acceleration stretches neuronal membranes and axons
K+ efflux, Na+ and Ca2+ influx
Glutamate release spreads depolarization
Na+/K+ ATPase and glucose use surge
Cerebral blood flow falls: energy crisis
Ion balance and flow recover over days to weeks
blocks.caption: Concussion is a temporary energy mismatch, not structural damage, which is why imaging stays normal.

blocks.text: Postconcussion syndrome is the persistence of these symptoms well beyond the usual recovery, often for months: headache, dizziness, fatigue, irritability, poor concentration and memory, insomnia, anxiety, and low mood. Imaging remains normal. The mechanism is not settled; lingering metabolic and microstructural axonal changes and psychological factors probably both contribute, and severity correlates poorly with the force of the original blow.

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), called dementia pugilistica when first described in boxers, is a progressive tauopathy linked to repeated head impacts, including many that never caused symptoms, in contact sports and military service. Its defining lesion is hyperphosphorylated tau in neurons, with or without astrocytes, clustered around small vessels at the depths of cortical sulci in a patchy pattern. The brain shows frontal and temporal atrophy, enlarged ventricles, a fenestrated cavum septum pellucidum, a thinned corpus callosum, and a pale substantia nigra. Clinically, mood and behavior change (depression, impulsivity, aggression) and memory loss progress to dementia, sometimes with parkinsonism, years after exposure ends. Diagnosis is confirmed only at autopsy. Alzheimer disease differs because its tangles begin in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus and are accompanied by amyloid plaques.

blocks.title: Three outcomes of head impact without a mass lesion
rows: Perivascular tau at sulcal depths, atrophy
Headache, dizziness, poor concentration, mood change
Behavior change, memory loss, dementia, parkinsonism
blocks.caption: All three can follow head impact with a normal acute CT; time course and tau pathology separate them.

sections.title: Coup and contrecoup contusion and diffuse axonal injury

blocks.text: A contusion is a bruise of the brain: blood leaks from small vessels into cortex that has struck the inside of the skull, with necrosis and edema around it. The crests of gyri touch bone first, so the hemorrhage is wedge-shaped with its base at the crest and the depths of sulci are relatively spared.

The brain floats in CSF and lags behind the skull when the head speeds up or stops. A coup contusion forms beneath the point of impact; a contrecoup contusion forms on the opposite side, where the brain strikes the skull as it rebounds. Coup lesions dominate when a stationary head is struck by a moving object. Contrecoup lesions are often the larger ones when a moving head hits a fixed surface, as in a fall backward onto the occiput that bruises the frontal and temporal poles. Whatever the impact site, the orbital frontal surfaces and anterior temporal poles are contused most, because they rest against the ridged orbital roofs, sphenoid wings, and middle cranial fossa. Injury there explains disinhibition, poor judgment, and personality change (orbitofrontal) and memory problems and seizures (temporal). Contusions can enlarge and swell over the first 1 to 3 days, and healed ones leave depressed yellow-brown scars at gyral crests (plaques jaunes) containing hemosiderin and gliosis.

Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is caused by rotational (angular) acceleration and deceleration, as in high-speed vehicle crashes, rather than by contact. Tissues of different density move at different rates, so shear concentrates at the gray-white junction, corpus callosum, internal capsule, and dorsolateral upper brainstem. Axons are rarely torn outright. Stretch disrupts the axolemma, admitting Ca2+ that activates proteases (calpains), which break down microtubules and neurofilaments. Fast axonal transport halts at the damaged point, transported organelles and proteins pile up, and within hours the axon swells into an axonal spheroid, then disconnects and undergoes Wallerian degeneration. Swellings are shown by immunostaining for amyloid precursor protein or by silver stains.

Because damage is spread through the hemispheric white matter and the reticular activating system of the upper brainstem, the patient is in coma from the moment of injury, yet CT shows no mass lesion and may be normal or show only small hemorrhages in the corpus callosum or dorsolateral brainstem. MRI is more sensitive. DAI is a leading cause of persistent coma or a vegetative state after trauma. A hematoma behaves differently: consciousness is lost later, as the mass expands.

blocks.title: Contusion versus diffuse axonal injury
rows: Axonal swellings, small white matter hemorrhages
Orbital frontal and anterior temporal poles
Gray-white junction, corpus callosum, dorsolateral brainstem
Coma from the moment of injury
Normal or nearly normal; no mass
Persistent coma or lasting cognitive disability
blocks.caption: Impact bruises the surface of the brain; rotation shears the axons deep within it.

blocks.predict: A driver in a high-speed rollover is unresponsive from the scene, but CT shows no hematoma or midline shift. What lesion explains this, and where would you expect to find it?
blocks.explain: Rotational shear stretches long axons, halting transport and producing axonal swellings in the corpus callosum and upper brainstem; disconnection of the reticular activating system and hemispheric white matter causes coma without a mass.

sections.title: The expanding hematoma: rising pressure, uncal herniation, and Duret hemorrhage

blocks.text: An epidural hematoma, usually from a fracture of the thin squamous temporal bone near the pterion that tears the middle meningeal artery, expands quickly under arterial pressure; in the classic pattern, seen in only a minority, a brief loss of consciousness is followed by a lucid interval of hours, then decline. An acute subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins collects more slowly. Either becomes a mass, and the sequence that follows is the same (the anatomy of each bleed is in NE-20-A).

The adult skull is a rigid box holding brain (about 80% of its volume), blood, and CSF (about 10% each). By the Monro-Kellie doctrine, an enlarging clot is first offset by displacing CSF into the spinal subarachnoid space and venous blood out of the skull, so intracranial pressure (ICP, normally about 5 to 15 mm Hg) barely rises. Once these reserves are used up, the pressure-volume curve turns steep and each added milliliter raises ICP sharply. This is why the patient can look well during the lucid interval: compensation is still holding ICP down. Because cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) equals mean arterial pressure (MAP) minus ICP, rising ICP lowers perfusion, and ischemic brain swells, which raises ICP further.

blocks.title: Vicious cycle of rising intracranial pressure
steps: Expanding clot adds volume to the fixed skull
CSF and venous reserves exhausted; ICP rises steeply
CPP (MAP minus ICP) falls
Brain ischemia causes cytotoxic edema
Edema adds volume and raises ICP further
blocks.caption: Once compensation is exhausted, ischemia and edema raise pressure faster than the clot alone.

blocks.text: Pressure gradients then push tissue across dural partitions. A lateral mass forces the medial temporal lobe (uncus and parahippocampal gyrus) through the tentorial notch, compressing midbrain-level structures in a predictable order. Parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibers run on the outer surface of the oculomotor nerve, so the ipsilateral pupil dilates and stops reacting before ptosis and a down-and-out eye appear.

blocks.title: Structures compressed in uncal herniation and the resulting signs
rows: Fixed dilated pupil, then ptosis and down-and-out eye
Cerebral peduncle (corticospinal fibers above the decussation)
Opposite peduncle against tentorial edge (Kernohan notch)
Infarct same side, field loss opposite
blocks.caption: The pupil marks the side of the mass more reliably than the weakness.

blocks.text: As the brainstem is pushed downward, the basilar artery, anchored to the circle of Willis, cannot follow. Its paramedian perforating branches tear, producing flame-shaped Duret hemorrhages in the midline midbrain and pons, a sign of terminal brainstem injury. Brainstem ischemia evokes the Cushing reflex: a sympathetic surge raises blood pressure, baroreceptors slow the heart, and breathing becomes irregular. Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum then compresses the medullary centers, causing apnea and death unless the clot is removed in time.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing a herniating hematoma
blocks.text: A 22-year-old is struck on the left side of the head, is dazed briefly, then talks normally for 3 hours before becoming drowsy. The left pupil is now dilated and unreactive and the right limbs are weak. Step 1: deterioration after a lucid interval points to a left epidural hematoma from a torn middle meningeal artery. Step 2: the left pupil fails first because the herniating left uncus presses on the outer, parasympathetic fibers of the left oculomotor nerve. Step 3: the left cerebral peduncle carries corticospinal fibers that have not yet crossed, so its compression weakens the right side.

blocks.predict: In the patient above, weakness appears on the left, the same side as the blown pupil. Has the mass moved?
blocks.explain: No. The midbrain is pushed against the opposite tentorial edge, compressing the right cerebral peduncle (Kernohan notch); the pupil still marks the side of the mass.
blocks.check: Compare with the uncal herniation table.

sections.title: Spinal cord transection: spinal shock, spasticity, and the level of injury

blocks.text: Complete transection severs every ascending and descending tract at one level. At the level itself, anterior horn cells and exiting roots are destroyed, giving lower motor neuron signs in that segment's muscles. Below it, motor neurons survive but lose all input from the brain. Sensation, voluntary movement, and conscious bladder and bowel control are lost below the lesion, and the picture below the level changes over time in two phases.

The first phase is spinal shock. Spinal motor neurons and interneurons depend on continuous facilitation from descending reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, and corticospinal fibers. When that input stops abruptly, they lose their resting excitability and stop responding, so everything below the level is flaccid and areflexic, including the bulbocavernosus reflex, and autonomic reflexes fail as well: the bladder is atonic with urinary retention and the gut develops ileus. It resembles a lower motor neuron lesion, but it is a temporary failure of neurons that are still intact.

With a lesion above about T6, neurogenic shock accompanies it. Sympathetic preganglionic neurons (T1 to L2) lose their brain input, so vascular tone falls and blood pools in the splanchnic and limb beds, while vagal output from the brainstem continues unopposed. The result is hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin, the opposite of the tachycardia and cold skin of hemorrhagic shock.

Over days to weeks, reflexes return, the bulbocavernosus reflex among the first, and then become exaggerated. Motor neurons below the lesion become intrinsically more excitable, denervated synapses become supersensitive, surviving segmental afferents sprout new connections, and descending inhibition is permanently gone. The result is the upper motor neuron picture: spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, clonus, and a Babinski sign. The bladder becomes reflexively spastic, often contracting against a sphincter that fails to relax (detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia). In lesions at or above T6, a stimulus below the level such as a distended bladder can trigger massive reflex sympathetic vasoconstriction (autonomic dysreflexia); baroreceptors respond by slowing the heart through the vagus and reducing sympathetic outflow above the lesion, which flushes the skin there, but this inhibition cannot descend past the cut, so hypertension persists.

blocks.title: Complete spinal cord transection over time
steps: Cord severed at one level
Descending facilitation lost; spinal neurons lose excitability
Spinal shock: flaccid, areflexic, atonic bladder
Above T6: neurogenic hypotension with bradycardia
Days to weeks: spinal reflexes return
Spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, spastic bladder
blocks.caption: The same lesion looks like a lower motor neuron injury at first and an upper motor neuron injury later.

blocks.text: The level decides breathing and limb function. The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5, mainly C4, so complete injury at or above C3 paralyzes the diaphragm and the patient cannot breathe without a ventilator. Lower cervical injury leaves the diaphragm working but paralyzes intercostal and abdominal muscles, reducing vital capacity and cough. Any complete cervical injury causes quadriplegia (tetraplegia); thoracic and lower injury spares the arms and causes paraplegia.

blocks.title: Level of complete cord injury and its consequences
rows: Diaphragm partly spared; breathing often weak and may need support
Quadriplegia with some arm function, more at lower levels
Diaphragm intact; intercostals lost, weak cough
Intercostal and abdominal loss lessens as level falls
blocks.caption: C3, C4, and C5 supply the phrenic nerve; the brachial plexus (C5 to T1) separates quadriplegia from paraplegia.

blocks.predict: Two days after a complete T4 transection, the legs are flaccid with absent reflexes. Will they stay that way?
blocks.explain: No. This is spinal shock from loss of descending facilitation; as spinal neurons regain and then exceed their excitability, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign appear over days to weeks.

sections.title: Spinal cord compression versus cauda equina syndrome

blocks.text: In adults the spinal cord ends at the conus medullaris at about the L1 to L2 vertebral level; below this, the thecal sac contains only the lumbar and sacral roots of the cauda equina. A mass above L1 compresses central tracts and produces upper motor neuron signs, while a mass below L2 compresses roots and produces lower motor neuron signs.

Spinal cord compression comes from an extradural mass pressing on the cord. Pressure first obstructs epidural venous drainage, causing congestion and vasogenic edema of the white matter, then reduces arterial flow, so ischemia and eventually infarction follow. Back pain is usually first, often for weeks; pain from vertebral metastasis is typically worse lying down and at night. Weakness of the legs follows, with a sensory level on the trunk, hyperreflexia, and Babinski signs. Bladder and bowel dysfunction tend to appear late. Rapid compression can cause initial flaccidity, similar to spinal shock, before upper motor neuron signs emerge.

Three causes dominate. Vertebral metastasis, most often from lung, breast, or prostate cancer (also kidney, lymphoma, and myeloma), grows from the vertebral body into the epidural space, most commonly in the thoracic spine. Spinal epidural abscess, usually Staphylococcus aureus, occurs mainly with injection drug use, diabetes, or recent spinal procedures and causes fever, back pain, and then deficit. Central disc herniation compresses the cord in the cervical or thoracic spine, whereas a large central lumbar disc (L4 to L5 or L5 to S1) compresses the cauda equina.

blocks.title: Metastatic spinal cord compression
steps: Hematogenous tumor seeds vertebral body
Tumor or collapsed bone enters epidural space
Epidural venous obstruction and vasogenic cord edema
Arterial flow falls; white matter ischemia
Weakness, sensory level, UMN signs, late bladder loss
Infarction makes the deficit permanent
blocks.caption: Compression injures the cord largely through venous congestion and ischemia, so deficits can progress over hours.

blocks.text: Cauda equina syndrome damages multiple lumbar and sacral roots. Loss of the S2 to S5 dermatomes gives saddle anesthesia over the perineum, buttocks, and inner thighs. The S2 to S4 roots carry parasympathetic fibers to the detrusor and the afferents of bladder filling, so the bladder fails to contract and urine is retained, with overflow incontinence. Loss of the S2 to S4 reflex arcs abolishes the anal wink and bulbocavernosus reflex and lowers anal sphincter tone. Because roots are lower motor neuron axons, the legs show flaccid, often asymmetric weakness, reduced or absent ankle reflexes, no Babinski sign, and radicular pain. Conus medullaris lesions sit between the two pictures.

blocks.title: Cord compression, conus medullaris lesion, and cauda equina syndrome
rows: Sacral cord at about L1 to L2
Lumbar and sacral roots below L2
Saddle anesthesia, often asymmetric; radicular pain
Retention with overflow; lost anal wink and tone
Metastasis, epidural abscess, cervical or thoracic disc
blocks.caption: Above the conus the lesion hits tracts (upper motor neuron); below it the lesion hits roots (lower motor neuron).

blocks.title: Worked example: tracts or roots?
blocks.text: A 64-year-old man with prostate cancer has 4 weeks of thoracic back pain, worse at night, then 2 days of leg weakness. He has brisk knee reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, and lost pinprick below the umbilicus. Step 1: upper motor neuron signs mean the cord itself is involved, above the conus. Step 2: a sensory level at the umbilicus (T10 dermatome) places the lesion at or above about T10. Step 3: night pain with prostate cancer points to vertebral metastasis. Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, a lax anal sphincter, and absent ankle reflexes would instead place the lesion in the cauda equina.

integration.text: In every trauma case, anatomy determines what tears, physiology determines what follows, and the time course shows which process is operating. Imaging measures structure, not function, so a normal CT can accompany a confused patient (concussion, metabolic failure) or a comatose one (diffuse axonal injury, microscopic shear). Herniation signs follow from where parasympathetic fibers lie on the oculomotor nerve and from corticospinal fibers crossing below the midbrain.

In the spinal cord, the segmental origin of the phrenic, sympathetic, and sacral parasympathetic outflows and the vertebral level where the cord ends predict breathing, blood pressure, and bladder function. Nontraumatic compression links this chapter to oncology (vertebral metastasis) and microbiology (Staphylococcus aureus epidural abscess). The main limit is time: spinal shock and the lucid interval both make an early examination look different from what the lesion will become.

summary: Concussion is a functional, metabolic injury (ion flux, glutamate surge, energy crisis with reduced blood flow) with normal CT and MRI.

Postconcussion syndrome is persistence of headache, dizziness, poor concentration, and mood change for months; chronic traumatic encephalopathy is a progressive tauopathy after repeated impacts, with perivascular tau at the depths of sulci.
Contusions occur at gyral crests beneath the impact (coup) and opposite it (contrecoup), most often in the orbital frontal and anterior temporal poles.
Diffuse axonal injury results from rotational shear; axonal swellings in the corpus callosum and upper brainstem cause coma without a mass on CT.
An expanding hematoma is compensated by displacing CSF and venous blood until reserve is exhausted, after which ICP rises steeply and CPP (MAP minus ICP) falls.
Uncal herniation compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (fixed dilated pupil first) and cerebral peduncle (contralateral hemiparesis); a Kernohan notch can give same-side weakness.
Downward brainstem shift tears paramedian basilar branches (Duret hemorrhages); the Cushing reflex and tonsillar herniation precede death unless the clot is removed.
Spinal shock (flaccid, areflexic, atonic bladder) gives way over days to weeks to spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski signs; lesions above about T6 cause neurogenic hypotension with bradycardia.
The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5, so complete injury at or above C3 requires a ventilator; cervical injury causes quadriplegia and thoracic injury paraplegia.

Cord compression gives back pain, a sensory level, and upper motor neuron signs; cauda equina syndrome gives saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, lost anal reflex, and lower motor neuron leg weakness.

verify: Typical concussion recovery time (days to a few weeks, longer in children and adolescents) and the duration that defines postconcussion syndrome (older definitions use 3 months; newer guidance uses persistent post-concussive symptoms beyond about 4 weeks) differ between sources; confirm which NABNE uses.

CTE neuropathologic criteria follow the NINDS and NIBIB consensus (2016, refined 2021); clinical diagnosis uses traumatic encephalopathy syndrome criteria. Confirm whether NABNE still uses the term dementia pugilistica.
Second impact syndrome is described cautiously here (a second blow during recovery causes disproportionate injury) because its existence as a distinct entity is debated.
The mechanism of Duret hemorrhage is usually given as tearing of paramedian basilar perforators; some authors propose venous obstruction or reperfusion as contributors.
Duration of spinal shock and the order in which reflexes return vary between sources (some describe four phases over about 12 months); values are given as days to weeks.

The level of the conus medullaris is about L1 to L2 in most adults, with anatomical range from about T12 to L3. The thoracic spine is the most common site of metastatic cord compression (about 60 to 70% in most series).
Saddle anesthesia is described as S2 to S5 or S3 to S5 dermatomes in different sources.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Kernohan notch, Duret hemorrhage, Cushing reflex, and plaques jaunes.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: herniation-syndromes (coronal brain showing subfalcine, uncal, central, and tonsillar herniation) and spinal-levels-cauda (sagittal spine showing the conus at L1 to L2, the cauda equina, and phrenic and brachial plexus levels).
